title: The Sehskriti's warnings
hook: wealth, youth and family are passing, it says (Salok Sehskriti)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Salok Sehskriti and their stately sound. Your line was the old tongue. Did you hear anyone dress their words up or down, and catch what they meant underneath? Day one thousand two hundred four.

Katanch. Katanch. Katanch. The word knocks like a hand on a door, again and again. It opens one of Guru Arjan's verses in the Salok Sehskriti, and roughly it asks: where is? who is? Where is the mother, where is the father, where is the wife, the son? A question asked so many times in a row stops being a question and becomes a drumbeat. Yesterday we listened to the old style. Today we hear what that style is used to say, and it's a plain warning.
screen: `KATANCH, KATANCH, KATANCH.` → `WHERE IS? WHO IS?` → `A QUESTION BECOMES A DRUMBEAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, paraphrased. Who is mother, who is father, who is wife, who are the children you delight in? Who are brother, friend, and kin, and what is the pull of the household? The bright, enchanting beauty of the world, you see it, and it leaves. What stays with you, Nanak says, is the remembrance of the Lord. The outline sums up the warnings of these verses in three words: wealth, youth, family. They pass. Now a careful note, because this is easy to mishear. Sikh teachers don't read this as a command to walk away from family. On this path we've seen Guru Ram Das build a town and pass the Guruship to his son, and Sikh teaching honors the householder's life. Katanch isn't asking whether your mother matters. It's asking where she can go with you, in the end, and where you can go with her. The answer is honest: not all the way. Every bond has a door it can't pass through. Some readers hear the verse less as a loss and more as a sorting. Love your people fully, it seems to say, and don't make them carry the weight only the Name can hold. That's the week, looking back. The fourth Guru's humble service and his way. The Bavan Akhri's letters, learning with heart, and an alphabet that ends in grace. The old tongue of the Sehskriti. And now its warning, knocking at the door.
screen: `WHO IS MOTHER, WHO IS FATHER?` · `NOT A COMMAND TO LEAVE HOME.` · `EVERY BOND HAS A DOOR.` · `THE WEEK, LOOKING BACK.` · then, large: `PASSING THINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one thing lightly. Choose something you love that will not last forever. A cup you use every morning. A season. Your own strength. Hold it in your mind, or in your hands if it's near. Don't push it away. Just loosen the grip a little, the way you'd hold a bird. Let yourself be grateful it's here, and honest that it passes. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each out-breath. The bell holds the time.
The Sehskriti's warnings. Mother, father, child, the world's bright beauty: they pass, this verse says; the remembrance of the Lord stays. Today's word.
Your line: passing things. That closes a week of letters and old tongues. Today, love one person well, and remember, without sadness, that the time is a gift. Day one thousand two hundred four.

howItsDone: Guru Arjan's Salok Sehskriti are read during a full reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and lines like these are often explained in katha, where gianis set the warnings about passing things beside the Sikh honor for family life.

match.prompt: inside the warning: tap the pairs.
pairs: bonds that can't go all the way
you see it, and it leaves

myth: the verse tells Sikhs to leave their families
the Gurus were householders; the verse asks where each bond can go with you, not whether it matters.
the verse names what stays when the rest passes
the remembrance of the Lord, Nanak says, stays with you.

fork.setup: the verse keeps knocking: where is mother, where is father, where is the child? what is it asking?
options: whether your family matters at all.
where each bond can go with you, and what stays to the end.
how to leave home and become an ascetic.
fork.reveal: katanch sorts rather than rejects: love your people fully, and remember that only the Name goes all the way.

original.note: where is? who is?: the knocking word that opens Guru Arjan's verse in the Salok Sehskriti.

trapdoor: what you thought: these warnings are gloomy about family.
what it means: they ask where each bond can go with you, and name what stays.
what a scholar hears: a householder Guru using a learned style to sort loves, not to renounce them.
recall: Guru Nanak's hymns on the invasion

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Salok Sehskriti Mahala 5 (katanch mata katanch pita), Ang 1353–1354
